terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation, intransitive; ex morbō, from an illness
evidence: M-O s.v. recover, get better, get well
terms.comment: The everyday word for getting well, in Cicero and the letters; also of plants and animals that thrive (Seneca, below). Those who are recovering are convalēscentēs (Plin. NH 20.34).

terms.grammar: the passive of recreō, with ex
evidence: Cic. Red. Quir. 4: ex gravī morbō (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 65, 369: ex gravī morbō recreārī, to recover from a serious illness
terms.comment: To be restored, refreshed: from a serious illness, a wound, weariness.
Traupman’s phrase, made of classical words: to get one’s health back.
Traupman’s word for getting over grief or anger, not an illness: to overcome it.

phrases.latin: nē aegrī quidem quia nōn omnēs convalēscunt, idcircō ars nūlla medicīna est
phrases.english: nor, because not all the sick recover, is medicine therefore no art

phrases.latin: nōn convalēscit planta quae saepe trānsfertur
phrases.english: a plant that is often moved does not thrive

phrases.latin: An convaluit? — Paulātim convalēscit, grātia Deō.
phrases.english: Has she recovered? — She’s slowly getting better, thank God.
to recover from a serious illness
